client: I've been really struggling lately with my thesis deadlines creeping up on me, and I honestly don't know how I'm going to get everything done in time. On top of that, I still have my part-time job and people expecting things from me socially, and it all just feels like too much at once. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the deadlines are still going to be there no matter what we discuss.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot right now — the thesis, work, social expectations all pressing in at once — and that kind of cumulative weight can make everything feel genuinely unmanageable. I hear your skepticism about talking too, and that's actually a really honest and important thing to name; you're right that the deadlines won't disappear, but what we *can* work on is how your mind is relating to all of this, which often changes what feels possible. What do you think is the loudest, most draining thought that keeps showing up when you think about everything on your plate?

client: The loudest thought is probably something like "I'm going to fail and let everyone down," and it just loops over and over whenever I try to sit down and actually work on the thesis. It's like the thought itself is so heavy that it actually stops me from doing anything, and then I feel even worse because time keeps passing and I haven't made progress. And then I feel guilty on top of that, which makes it even harder to start.
therapist: That thought — "I'm going to fail and let everyone down" — sounds exhausting to carry, especially when it becomes a wall between you and the very work you need to do, creating this painful cycle of guilt and paralysis. In CBT we'd call this a kind of cognitive trap, where the thought itself becomes the obstacle more than the actual thesis does. I'm curious — when that thought shows up, whose voices or faces come to mind when you imagine "letting everyone down"?

client: Honestly, the first face that comes to mind is my supervisor's — I imagine that look of disappointment when I have to admit I haven't made enough progress. But then it's also my parents, because they've sacrificed a lot to support me through this degree and I feel like I owe them something. It's weird because even my friends show up in that image, even though they haven't actually put any pressure on me at all.
therapist: It's really meaningful that you can see so clearly who's in that image — and it's especially interesting that your friends appear there even though they haven't actually asked anything of you, which suggests part of this pressure might be coming from inside rather than from the people around you. That's not a criticism at all — it actually points to something important: your mind may be generating expectations on behalf of others that they haven't even expressed. If you were to check in with your supervisor or your parents about what they actually expect from you right now, how do you think that might differ from what you're imagining?

client: Rationally, I know my supervisor has probably seen students struggle before and my parents just want me to be okay, but actually having those conversations feels terrifying to me. Like, what if checking in with my supervisor just makes it more real, or she starts questioning whether I'm capable of finishing at all? I think part of me would rather keep assuming the worst privately than risk confirming it out loud.
therapist: There's something really understandable about that — keeping the fear private feels safer than risking having it confirmed, but it also means you're essentially living inside the worst-case scenario already, without any of the actual information that might contradict it. Your rational mind already knows your supervisor and parents are likely more supportive than the story you're telling yourself, and that gap between what you *know* and what you *feel* is really worth exploring. What do you think it would mean about you as a person if your supervisor did express some concern — would that actually confirm you're incapable, or might it mean something else entirely?

client: I guess logically it wouldn't mean I'm incapable, it would just mean I'm struggling with something hard, which is probably true for most PhD students. But in the moment, my brain doesn't really make that distinction — it just hears "concern" and translates it directly into "you're not good enough." I can see what you're trying to do with this reframe, but I'm not sure I can just think my way out of a feeling that's been with me for so long.
therapist: You're making a really sharp observation — and you're absolutely right that reframing alone rarely dissolves a feeling that's been woven into your sense of self for a long time, so I don't want to oversell it as a quick fix. What CBT actually aims for isn't forcing yourself to *think* differently in the moment, but gradually building enough small experiences that contradict the old belief until the feeling starts to shift on its own. I'm wondering — can you think of even one moment, maybe from earlier in your degree, where you struggled but ultimately showed you *were* capable enough?

client: There was this one seminar paper in my second year where I was completely convinced I was going to fail it, and I ended up getting really positive feedback from the professor. But when I try to hold onto that memory right now, it feels distant and almost irrelevant, like my brain is saying "that was then, this is bigger and different." I can acknowledge it happened, but I don't know how to make it actually feel like evidence of anything useful right now.
therapist: It's actually really significant that you found that memory, even if it feels muted right now — your brain's tendency to dismiss it as "different" is itself a pattern worth noticing, because it will likely do the same thing with *this* thesis once you get through it too. That discounting move — "yes, but this time is different" — is one of the ways the "not good enough" belief protects itself from being challenged, so the fact that you can see it happening is genuinely useful. I'm curious, if a close friend came to you with that same seminar paper memory and said it felt irrelevant, what would you say to them about whether it counted as real evidence?

client: If a friend said that to me, I'd probably tell them that of course it counts, that it shows they've handled pressure before and came through it. But it's so much easier to be generous and logical with someone else than it is with myself, and I'm not sure why that gap exists or how to close it. It almost makes me feel worse in a way, because now I can see I'm being unfair to myself but I still can't seem to stop doing it.
therapist: That moment of recognition — seeing the double standard clearly but feeling unable to bridge it — can actually feel like a new kind of frustration on top of everything else, and I want to acknowledge that's a really hard place to sit. But I'd gently offer that noticing the gap *is* the first step to closing it; you can't change a pattern you can't see, and you're seeing it now with real clarity. I'm wondering — what do you think gets in the way of extending that same generosity to yourself, is there something that feels unsafe or even wrong about treating yourself the way you'd treat a friend?

client: Honestly, I think part of me believes that being hard on myself is what keeps me working, like if I let up on the self-criticism then I'll just stop trying altogether. There's almost a superstitious quality to it, like the self-punishment is the thing holding everything together, and being kind to myself feels dangerously close to giving up or making excuses. I know that probably sounds irrational when I say it out loud, but it's a really deeply held feeling.
therapist: What you just described doesn't sound irrational at all — it actually makes a lot of sense as a strategy your mind developed at some point, probably because self-criticism *did* feel like it was keeping you safe or moving forward. But there's a really important thing to gently test here: the evidence from your own life, like that seminar paper, suggests you pushed through difficulty and succeeded *despite* the self-criticism, not necessarily because of it. What if the drive to finish your thesis is actually coming from something more like genuine care about your work or your future, rather than the self-punishment — do you think there's any part of you that wants to finish this for reasons beyond just avoiding failure?

client: Yeah, I think there is a part of me that actually cares about the research itself, like there are moments when I'm deep in the work and I genuinely find it interesting and meaningful. But it's hard to access that feeling when the anxiety is loud, and I worry that if I start focusing on "I care about this" instead of "I have to do this or else," I'll somehow lose the urgency I need to meet the deadline. It feels risky to swap out the thing that's been driving me, even if that thing is also hurting me.
therapist: That genuine curiosity and care you just described — those moments of being absorbed in the work itself — is actually a much more sustainable fuel than fear, and research on motivation backs this up pretty strongly. The anxiety feels urgent, but it's also the very thing that's been freezing you at your desk, so it may be less reliable as a driver than it seems. I'm wondering if we could think of this not as swapping one thing for another, but as experimenting — what might it feel like to try connecting to that genuine interest for even a small, contained work session, and see whether the urgency you need actually disappears or perhaps just changes shape?

client: I like the idea of framing it as an experiment rather than a permanent switch, that feels a bit less threatening. But I'm worried that in practice, the moment I sit down to work, the anxiety is just going to flood in anyway and drown out any sense of curiosity before I even get started. How do I actually access that genuine interest when the first thing that shows up is panic?
therapist: That's such a practical and important question, and it shows you're already thinking about implementation rather than just insight, which is a real shift. One CBT-informed approach is to create a tiny "on-ramp" before you sit down to write — something like spending just two or three minutes reading a part of your research that you've previously found genuinely interesting, not to produce anything, but just to let curiosity show up before the pressure does. What do you think — is there a specific part of your thesis topic, even a single idea or question, that still has a little spark of interest attached to it when you imagine it right now?
